A Japanese novelist, poet and lady-in-waiting at the imperial court in the Heian period, who wrote The Tale of Genji in about 1000 to 1012. It is often called one of the world's first novels. Murasaki Shikibu is a nickname; her real name is unknown.

She grew up in the household of a scholar of the Fujiwara family. Girls were not supposed to learn Chinese, the written language of government, but she picked it up by listening to her brother's lessons. She married in her twenties and was widowed after about two years. She probably began Genji around then.

In about 1005 the powerful regent Fujiwara no Michinaga brought her to court to serve his daughter, Empress Shoshi, likely because of her fame as a writer. She kept writing there and also left a diary of court life. Scholars disagree on when she died; dates from 1014 to 1025 have been proposed.

Genji follows the loves and losses of a handsome prince across 54 chapters. It is famous for its close attention to feeling, mood and the passing of time. It was written in kana, the Japanese script that let court women write in their own language, while men wrote mostly in Chinese. With Sei Shonagon's Pillow Book, it marks the peak of the women's literature of Heian Japan.

The book has been read, illustrated and retold ever since, from picture scrolls to modern manga, and it remains a centre of Japanese literature.
